title: A Forgotten Forest Experiment Grew Giant Trees
summary:
How should people take care of a forest? In Australia, people have argued about this for decades. Some want forests fully protected. Others want trees harvested for wood to support local jobs. A long-forgotten experiment suggests there may be a middle path.

In the late 1980s, the government of the Australian state of Victoria set up a big experiment in its mountain ash forests. Mountain ash trees are among the tallest trees in the world. Scientists tried different ways of harvesting. Some areas were clearfelled, meaning every tree in a block was cut down. Others had small patches cleared. In "heavily thinned" areas, 50 to 70 percent of the trees were cut, and the rest were left standing. Some forest was left untouched for comparison.

After early results were published, the experiment was forgotten. The access road grew over and the project sign fell down. Then, in 2014, researchers from the University of Melbourne visited the site with students and were amazed by what they found.

The trees left behind in the thinned areas had grown enormous, with more space and resources to share. The largest averaged more than a meter across and were 20 percent wider than the biggest trees in untouched forest. Even more surprising, the thinned forest had stored as much carbon in its wood as the untouched forest, or more.

Bigger trees are more likely to survive fires and to form hollows, where rare animals such as the greater glider live. Camera traps found endangered Leadbeater's possums in every harvested plot the team surveyed, but none in the untouched areas.

The researchers say careful thinning could provide wood, store carbon and help wildlife at the same time, though it should not be done everywhere.
why_it_matters: The findings suggest forests can be managed to provide wood, store carbon and support wildlife at the same time, which could inform decisions about forests.
